Where it began

Imran Khan's story starts in Lahore, where he was born on 5 October 1952. He went to school at Aitchison College in his home city, then crossed to England for a spell at the Royal Grammar School in Worcester. By then he had already made his first-class debut in Lahore, at 16.

From there he went up to Keble College, Oxford, and won his Blue in the university side between 1973 and 1975. Alongside his studies he played county cricket for Worcestershire, and later turned out for Sussex from 1983 to 1988.

The player

His first Test came against England at Edgbaston in June 1971. He became one of the finest fast bowlers of his era, and twice won the Wetherell Award as the leading all-rounder in the English first-class game. Between 1980 and 1988 he took 236 Test wickets at only 17.77 apiece. His best figures, 8 for 58, came against Sri Lanka.

In all he played 88 Tests, took 362 wickets at 22.81 with 23 five-wicket innings, and made 3,807 runs at 37.69 with six hundreds. He reached the double of 3,000 runs and 300 wickets in just 75 Tests. In 1983 he became the second man, after Ian Botham, to make a hundred and take ten wickets in the same Test.

What made him special

He was a thinker as well as a bowler. He learned the art of reverse swing from Sarfraz Nawaz and then handed it on to Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis, which may be the most valuable gift one fast bowler has ever given to two others. Made captain in 1982, he led Pakistan that summer to their first Test win in England for 28 years, and in 1987 to their first Test series wins in India and in England. He finished with the 1992 World Cup, top-scoring in the final and taking the last wicket himself.

He also pushed for neutral umpires long before the rules required them, inviting officials from India and England to stand in home series. And he could bat. From number six in the order he averaged 61.86, one of the best records anyone has managed there.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year in 1983, Pakistan gave him the Pride of Performance, and in 2009 he entered the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame. After his playing days he worked as a commentator and served as UNICEF's Special Representative for Sports. He became chancellor of the University of Bradford in 2005 and helped found Namal College in Mianwali, which opened in 2008. He later went into public life and served as Prime Minister of Pakistan.

And finally

His teams were very hard to beat. Of the 48 Tests in which he led Pakistan, they lost only eight, and 26 ended in a draw. After a cloudburst hit Islamabad in 2001, he auctioned his own bat from that 1992 World Cup to help those affected. It raised US$20,000, a fair return on a bat that had already done plenty.
